newsitem.title: JAPAN: Oil prices, dollar jump on news of missile attack.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices, dollar jump on news of missile attack.

text.p: Crude oil prices and the dollar jumped in Asia on Tuesday on news that the U.S. military had launched cruise missile strikes against air-defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.

New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) crude oil prices for October jumped 22 cents per barrel to $23.70 immediately after the Pentagon announced the United States had fired the missiles at Iraq, traders said.
The dollar also climbed immediately on news of the attacks, but settled back in later trade, dealers said.

Gold prices rose marginally while the Tokyo Stock Exchange, which had been affected only slightly by earlier media reports an attack could take place, was just closing at 3 p.m. (0600 GMT) when news of the attack came out.
NYMEX crude prices trade on an after-hours screen system called ACCESS outside New York trading hours.
The prompt October contract was at $23.48 and jumped to $23.70 on the news.
In Singapore, Simex Brent futures for October touched a high of $23.50 on news of the attack, up from a London Brent close of $21.99.

The dollar was standing higher in late Tokyo trade on Tuesday, but was off earlier highs as heavy sales mainly from Japanese exporters crushed a brief rally triggered by the U.S. missile attack on Iraq, dealers said.
In late afternoon trade, the dollar was at about 109.15 yen, after jumping briefly to about 109.35 on news of the attack.
Gold prices in Tokyo rose slightly after the Pentagon announcement with spot gold a tad higher at $387.10/387.60 an ounce from $386.65/387.15 in London on Monday.
Tokyo stocks swung back into positive territory by the close on Tuesday afternoon with the market not having a chance to react to the news of the missile attack, brokers said.
The key 225-share Nikkei average closed up 91.04 points or 0.45 percent at 20,198.15 after earlier dropping as low as 19,920.02 in early morning trade.

"The market could not digest the news before the close," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd. "We have to wait for further developments and its impact on Wall Street."

The U.S. Defense Department gave no further immediate details of the attacks. But U.S. defence officials, who asked not to be identified, said the unmanned and highly accurate missiles were fired from B-52 bombers and American warships in the Gulf at air defence command and control military targets in and around Baghdad.
The Pentagon said the raids were launched on orders from President Bill Clinton.

"At the direction of the president, the Department of Defense has launched cruise missiles to attack selected air defence targets in Iraq. No further details are available at this time," the brief announcement said.
